title: Sublattice-resolved coherent phonon dynamics in charge density waves
authors: Kyoung Hun Oh, Honglie Ning, Zongqi Shen, Yifan Su, Jack Maier, Gyeongbo Kang, Hyeongi Choi, Dong Wu, Qiaomei Liu, Hyun-Woo J. Kim, Seunghyeok Ha, Jaehwon Kim, Byungjune Lee, B. J. Kim, N. L. Wang, Yao Wang, Hoyoung Jang, Nuh Gedik
abstract: Phonons govern fundamental material properties and play a central role in various electronic phase transitions. Coherent driving of specific phonon modes enables on-demand phase control, motivating sublattice-resolved identification of real-space phonon motions. Yet experimentally resolving these motions remains challenging, limiting precise phonon-based control. Here, we introduce a dynamical protocol to track element-resolved phonon dynamics in the charge density wave material EuTe4, in which the dominant Te-sublattice charge order is accompanied by a previously unreported Eu-sublattice component. We leverage the elemental selectivity of time-resolved resonant X-ray scattering to reveal three coherent phonon modes with distinct sublattice character, thereby disentangling Eu- and Te-dominated lattice dynamics, in good agreement with theoretical calculations of the phonon eigenvectors. This time-domain approach, which surpasses the energy-resolution limits of conventional frequency-domain inelastic scattering, provides a broadly applicable framework for decomposing coherent phonons in multi-element materials, which is crucial for the targeted control of phases of matter.
summary: The research reports on using time-resolved resonant X-ray scattering ($	ext{tr-RXS}$) to overcome the challenge of resolving sublattice-specific phonon motions in charge density wave materials. By exploiting element selectivity via tunable X-ray energies, the authors successfully decoupled and identified three distinct coherent phonon modes in $	ext{EuTe}_4$, assigning them definitively to either Te or Eu lattice vibrations.
main_problem: The primary challenge is experimentally resolving sublattice-specific phonon motions within multi-element materials that exhibit charge density waves (CDWs).
main_result: The authors successfully disentangled three distinct coherent phonon modes ($\sim 0.85, 1.3, 	ext{ and } 1.6 	ext{ THz}$) in $	ext{EuTe}_4$, assigning them to specific Eu- or Te-dominated lattice dynamics.
method: They utilized time-resolved resonant X-ray scattering ($	ext{tr-RXS}$), a time-domain approach, which surpasses the energy resolution limits of conventional inelastic scattering techniques.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the CDW material $	ext{EuTe}_4$, which has alternating Te monolayers and EuTe slabs. The analysis models the measured intensity as a weighted sum of contributions from the two distinct sublattices (Te and Eu).
key_observables: Coherent phonon frequencies ($\sim 0.85, 1.3, 	ext{ and } 1.6 	ext{ THz}$), element-resolved lattice dynamics, and CDW diffraction intensity oscillations.
important_parameters: The technique relies on tuning the X-ray probe energy near specific elemental absorption edges (e.g., Eu $M_{5,4}$ edges) to achieve elemental selectivity.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the measured signal can be accurately modeled as a linear combination of independent sublattice contributions whose weights depend strongly on the probe energy.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the $	ext{tr-RXS}$ experimental setup, showing time evolution and FFTs of CDW intensity oscillations at different probe energies. Subsequent figures detail the quantitative decoupling process using the two-sublattice model to assign specific phonon modes to Eu or Te motion.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem (lack of sublattice resolution), details the $	ext{tr-RXS}$ methodology, presents time-domain measurements showing oscillations, and finally uses FFT analysis combined with a multi-energy fitting model to decouple and assign specific phonon modes to their respective sublattices.
why_interesting: This work demonstrates an advanced spectroscopic technique ($	ext{tr-RXS}$) capable of providing element-specific structural dynamics information in correlated materials, which is highly relevant for understanding lattice coupling mechanisms central to many quantum phenomena.
